kicker: Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing · fix report
title: Catch Card Fix
lede: On an iPhone the card that shows a catch covered part of the fish you hold up: the back half on its side, the lower half upright. The fish is now held up in the middle of the part of the screen the card leaves free, further out when it is big, and the small map, compass and goal step aside while the card is up. Of 639 cases (71 fish on 9 screen shapes), 484 had part of the fish under the card before and 0 after; 11 of 11 regression scenarios ran clean and an independent review's three findings were fixed.

sections.title: What was asked
sections.html:
The request: "On iPhone the info screen of the fish I covering the screen so can only see the upper part of the fish".

AskedWhat was doneStatus
On iPhone the info screen of the fish is covering the screen so can only see the upper part of the fishThe card that shows a catch sat over the fish you hold up: on its side the card covered the back half of the fish, held upright it covered the lower half, and upright the bigger fish were also wider than the screen. The fish is now held up in the part of the screen the card leaves free, all of it in view, on every iPhone, iPad and desktop shape tested.Fixed
Found while fixing itWith the fish moved, the small map, the compass and the goal took the room above the card when upright; they now step aside while the card is up and come back with it. The trophy photo framed the fish from the middle of the screen; it still does, as the fish is put in the middle of the picture for the one frame the photo keeps.Done
Checked639 cases (71 fish on 9 screen shapes): 484 had part of the fish under the card before, 0 after. Pictures before and after on all 9 shapes, 11 regression scenarios on the final build (11 clean), and an independent code review whose three findings were all fixed.Done

sections.title: Why the card covered the fish
sections.html:
When a fish is landed, the game shows the fish held up in both hands and a card with its name, weight, length and value, and the KEEP and RELEASE buttons. The two were placed without regard for each other:

  • The fish was always held in the middle of the view, at a distance that grows with its length, whatever the screen's shape.
  • The card is a fixed panel: on a screen on its side it sits on the right, about 300 points wide on a phone plus its margin: more than a third of an iPhone's width, close to half with the island's inset; upright it sits along the bottom, across the whole width.
  • Upright, the view is narrow. The game keeps the view 88 degrees tall, which leaves it 48 degrees wide on an iPhone, so a king salmon held at its usual distance (about a metre) is wider than the screen.

So on its side the card covered the back half of a big fish, and upright it covered the lower half: the upper part was all that showed. The pictures are from the game drawn at an iPhone's shape, before and after.

sections.title: Holding the fish where the card leaves room
sections.html:
Five parts, each small:

  1. The card says where it leaves room. When it shows, and whenever the screen changes shape, the game measures where the card ends up once it has slid in, the screen's safe area (clear of the island, the rounded corners and the home bar) and the bottom of the money, health and buttons along the top. What is left of the card and what is above it are the rooms for the fish.
  2. The fish is held up in the middle of a room. A box round the fish and the hands on it is projected onto the screen and moved until it sits in the middle of the room. If it is too big for the room at its usual distance, it is held further out until it fits, at most 2.2 times as far. Of the rooms, the one that shows the fish biggest is used: left of the card on a screen on its side, above it upright. It glides to a new place if the phone is turned with the card up.
  3. The small map, the compass and the goal step aside while the card is up (they hold their place, so nothing else moves) and come back when you keep or release the fish. Upright they took most of the room above the card.
  4. The arms reach. The sleeves of the two arms that hold a catch ran 48 cm from the wrist, just past the bottom of the view; held further out, their open ends would have shown. They now run on another 1.5 metres at the same width, out of the view in every case tested. The other arms (the rod, the bow, the paraglider, climbing) are built exactly as before.
  5. The trophy photo still frames the fish. A photo keeps a 16 by 9 frame from the middle of the screen. For the one frame the photo keeps, under the white flash, the fish is placed in the middle of that frame, held further out if it is too big for it, then goes back beside the card.

sections.title: 71 fish on 9 screens
sections.html:
A check in the game (now the regression scenario catch-room) holds up every fish in turn, each species at its smallest and its largest weight and each legendary fish, 71 in all, on nine screen shapes, and measures the box round the fish and the hands against the card, the safe area, the bars along the top and the photo's frame, and where the sleeves end. "Under the card" counts the fish whose box overlaps the card at all; "worst" is how much of that box the card covered.

After the fix no fish is under the card, outside the safe area or under the bars along the top in any of the 639 cases, and no sleeve end is in sight. The photo still cuts the largest flatfish and skates when held upright, where the photo's 16 by 9 frame is a thin band across a tall screen; much less than before. "Held out" is the distance the fish is held at against its usual one.

sections.title: What it costs
sections.html:
No new draw calls, materials, textures or shader programs. Per frame, while a fish is held up, the fit projects eight corners a few dozen times: 10.3 microseconds a frame here (1 room), in a software-drawn page that is several times slower than a phone. The card and the top bars are measured once when the card shows and once on each change of the screen's shape, not every frame.

Arm holding a catchTriangles beforeAfterChange
The hand holding the tail6 3089 308+3 000
The hand under the belly6 3089 308+3 000

The longer sleeves are drawn only while a fish is held up, and most of their length is outside the view. The other arms (the rod hand, the bow hand, the drawing hand, both hands on the paraglider and both climbing hands) are built exactly as before: the same triangles, and a fingerprint of every vertex position is the same in both builds for all 7.

Regression scenarios on the final build

Clean: the scenario ran to its end with no page error, failed step or error printed by the page.

One picture needed a closer look: in camera, the compass and the goal still show in the first frame after the card appears. That scenario runs with reduced motion, and the game's reduced-motion rule gives every change of style a transition of a hundredth of a millisecond, which ends with the next frame drawn; the software renderer draws about one frame a second, so the picture caught that frame. The next frame has them hidden, and on a phone that one frame lasts a sixtieth of a second. Setting the hiding on each element instead was tried and behaves the same, so the simpler rule stayed.

Its first run printed FAIL for three shapes, with the numbers of the shape before: the check had run before the game took the new shape, as a slow software frame holds the browser's resize event back for seconds. The scenario now waits until the game has resized (which also measures the card again) before it checks. The check also measures the card where it rests, as the game does: read live, the card can be caught partway through its 20-point slide-in in the software renderer, which had made a few of the "before" counts too low. The game was not changed for either. The lines above are from the final run, and they agree with the nine separate checks in the numbers section.

The independent code review

A separate review read the change against the game: the conversions between the screen's points and the view, the card's slide-in, the safe-area probe, every way the card or the fish can go away (keeping, releasing, a bear, fast travel, going back to the title, the eagle), the photo's frame, the first frame, the cost per frame and the other arms. It found these three things, all fixed:

SeverityFoundWhat was done
MediumMeasuring the card set its slide-in animation aside and back, which starts it again. The game measures again on every resize, and resizes itself on each automatic resolution step and quality drop, so on a phone with slow frames the card would fade out and slide in again while you read it, and turning the phone replayed it twice.Only a slide still running is set aside for the measure; one already over is left alone. Checked in the catch-room scenario, which turns the screen through seven shapes with the card up.
LowWhen a fish was too big for every room even at the furthest hold, the rooms tied and the one nearer the usual place won, which could be the one the fish spilled out of more.The fit now also reports how much the fish still spills over, and of two rooms that tie on distance the one it spills out of least wins. No screen tested needs it: every fish fits.
NitThe sleeve's new shaped length divided and multiplied back, which can differ from the old value in the last binary place for the existing arms.The existing arms now take the old value exactly, so they are built bit for bit as before.

sections.title: What this report cannot show
sections.html:
• No real iPhone was used. The pictures come from Chromium drawing in software at an iPhone's shape, with an iPhone's browser name. The island's insets were set by hand to the iPhone 15's values, and Safari's bars by a shorter view; a real phone may differ by a few points.
  • A big fish now looks smaller. To fit, the biggest fish are held up to 1.6 times as far out on a phone on its side and up to 1.9 times upright; the hands shrink with them, as they would. They show whole instead of large.
  • The small map, the compass and the goal are hidden while the card is up. The view is held still on the catch until you keep or release it, so they have nothing new to show in that time.
  • The photo upright still cuts the biggest skates and halibut a little (see the numbers): a 16 by 9 picture is a thin band across an upright phone.
  • Sources were read through web search. curl is blocked for every host in this environment, so the pages below were found and summarised by search, not downloaded in full. To allow hosts: the cloud environment menu in the session's title bar, then Edit, then Network access (a broader level, or Custom with the hosts added under Allowed domains); the steps are at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments#network-access.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
The conclusion: the card no longer covers the fish. On every screen shape tested, on its side or upright, every fish in the game is held up whole in the part of the screen the card leaves free, with nothing else of the game in the way, and the trophy photo still frames it. This conclusion would change if:

  • On your iPhone a fish still runs under the card. The room is measured from the card itself, so a different card size is allowed for; a screenshot would show whether the safe area or a bar along the top is measured differently on the phone.
  • Your view is shorter than the shortest one tested. The shortest here was 340 points tall on its side (Safari with its bars showing), where every fish fitted at no more than 1.6 times its usual distance. On a shorter view the biggest fish are held further out, up to 2.2 times, and past that would spill over the edges of the room, the card's side included.
  • You would rather see the fish big than whole. The other way is a smaller card on a phone (the description line hidden, say), which leaves more room; it is a change to the card, not to the fit.

footer:
Built on the claude/ruben-hotrod-fishing branch: the code on GitHub, the README and the playable build. The room is measured in src/ui/hud.js (measureCatch), the fish is placed in src/entities/viewmodel.js (fishFit), the sleeves are built in src/entities/hands.js, and the check is tools/scenarios/catch-room.json.

Sources. The iPhone 15's screen in points (393 by 852) and its safe-area insets on its side (59 left and right, 21 at the bottom) and upright (59 at the top, 34 at the bottom): Use Your Loaf, iPhone 15 Screen Sizes, https://useyourloaf.com/blog/iphone-15-screen-sizes/ · Safari's bars change the height a page gets: Apple Developer Forums, window.innerHeight is incorrect in Safari iPhone/iPad, https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/735055 · The safe-area insets a page reads with env(): MDN, env(), https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/env · Using the safe-area environment variables: MDN, Using environment variables, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_environment_variables/Using_environment_variables · Where an element is on the screen, transforms included: MDN, Element.getBoundingClientRect(), https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/getBoundingClientRect · The animations running on an element: MDN, Element.getAnimations(), https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/getAnimations · Hiding an element and its taps while keeping its place: MDN, visibility, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/visibility · The box round the fish: three.js, Box3, https://threejs.org/docs/pages/Box3.html · The view's field of view is the vertical one: three.js, PerspectiveCamera, https://threejs.org/docs/pages/PerspectiveCamera.html.
